episodes.title: 90 minutes of unfiltered product advice from Snap and Discord’s product chief | Peter Sellis
episodes.description:
Peter Sellis was the first product manager at Snapchat, where he spent seven years building one of the most beloved consumer products in history. He went on to serve as Head of Product at Discord, where he helped drive some of the fastest user growth the platform had seen. Having left his role at Discord, he gets to be especially real and unfiltered — nothing to promote, no PR, no comms team.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Peter designs teams like . . . terrorist organizations
2. What it was really like to manage Nikita Bier
3. Why the median PM is so bad
4. Why Snapchat’s ads business never reached its potential
5. Why growth almost always comes from the core product
6. Peter’s three “oxymorons” of great product management
episodes.descriptionCN:
Peter Sellis 是 Snapchat 的第一位产品经理，他花了七年时间打造了历史上最受欢迎的消费产品之一。他后来担任 Discord 的产品主管，帮助推动了该平台有史以来最快的用户增长。离开 Discord 后，他变得特别真实、未经过滤——没有什么可宣传的，没有公关，没有传播团队。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么彼得设计这样的团队。 。 。恐怖组织
2. 管理尼基塔·比尔的真实感受
3. 为什么 PM 中位数如此糟糕
4. 为什么 Snapchat 的广告业务从未发挥出潜力
5. 为什么增长几乎总是来自核心产品
6. Peter 关于优秀产品管理的三个“矛盾修辞法”

episodes.title: How we built Grok Bot in a month | Roman Ugarte (SpaceXAI)
episodes.description:
Roman Ugarte helped incubate and build Grok Bot, the popular new knowledge-work agent from SpaceXAI. A small, isolated team took it from first line of code to a working internal product in four weeks, and to a hugely successful public launch just three weeks later. Before Grok Bot, Roman led Growth at Cursor, where he helped scale the company from 15 people to over 1,000 before its acquisition by SpaceX.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. The origin story of Grok Bot
2. The key decision to build it from scratch instead of adding it to Cursor
3. Why the team personally onboarded nearly 300 of its first users
4. The two early product decisions that made Grok Bot so successful
5. Their “colleague-pilled” product philosophy
6. Roman’s advice on moats, and what has allowed Cursor to keep winning in the most competitive market in the world
episodes.descriptionCN:
Roman Ugarte 帮助孵化和构建了 Grok Bot，这是 SpaceXAI 推出的流行的新型知识工作代理。一个小型、孤立的团队在四个星期内将其从第一行代码变成了一个可运行的内部产品，并在三周后取得了巨大成功的公开发布。在加入 Grok Bot 之前，Roman 领导了 Cursor 的发展，在该公司被 SpaceX 收购之前，他帮助该公司从 15 人扩大到 1,000 多人。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. Grok Bot 的起源故事
2.关键决定是从头开始构建它而不是添加到Cursor中
3. 为什么团队亲自吸引了近 300 名第一批用户
4. 让 Grok Bot 如此成功的两个早期产品决策
5. 他们的“同事堆积”的产品理念
6. Roman 关于护城河的建议，以及是什么让 Cursor 在全球竞争最激烈的市场中不断获胜

episodes.title: Why companies are becoming a series of loops | Anish Acharya (a16z)
episodes.description:
Anish Acharya is a General Partner at Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), where he has focused on consumer investing. Anish is one of the most insightful, thought-provoking, and in-the-weeds product investors I’ve met, and this conversation will get your mind buzzing. Before joining a16z, Anish was a serial founder and operator: he founded SocialDeck, which he sold to Google, then led multiple efforts inside Google before founding Snowball, which he sold to Credit Karma. At Credit Karma he rose to VP of Product and then GM of the consumer product and the broader credit card business.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why you don’t have to worry about becoming part of the “permanent underclass”
2. Why company building will now involve creating a series of loops
3. What’s happening in consumer right now
4. Why the biggest opportunity in consumer is “/loop, make me happier”
5. Why moats are discovered, not designed
6. The rising importance of distribution as a moat
7. Being a model sommelier
episodes.descriptionCN:
Anish Acharya 是 Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) 的普通合伙人，专注于消费者投资。安尼什是我见过的最有洞察力、最发人深省、最活跃的产品投资者之一，这次谈话会让你头脑发热。在加入 a16z 之前，Anish 是一位连续创始人和运营商：他创立了 SocialDeck，并将其卖给了 Google，然后在 Google 内部领导了多项工作，最后创立了 Snowball，并将其卖给了 Credit Karma。在 Credit Karma，他升任产品副总裁，然后担任消费产品和更广泛的信用卡业务总经理。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么你不必担心成为“永久下层阶级”的一部分
2. 为什么公司建设现在需要创建一系列循环
3. 消费者现在正在发生什么
4. 为什么消费者最大的机会是“/loop，让我更快乐”
5. 为什么护城河是被发现的，而不是设计的
6. 分销作为护城河的重要性日益增加
7. 成为模范侍酒师

episodes.title: AI’s third era: the rise of persistent AI coworkers | Tara Seshan (Product Lead ChatGPT Work)
episodes.description:
Tara Seshan leads product for Codex and ChatGPT Work at OpenAI (alongside previous podcast guest Andrew Ambrosino, who’s her engineering manager). Before OpenAI, Tara spent over six years at Stripe, where she joined as one of the first five product managers. She went on to lead product for Watershed, which Time magazine named one of the best inventions of 2022, and she is also a founder and Thiel Fellow. Most personally meaningful to me: Tara is one of the three inaugural Lenny’s Newsletter Fellows, a program I ran a couple of years ago to spotlight the most exciting up-and-coming product leaders.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. The shift from “rowing” to “steering,” and why human judgment and ambition will become differentiators as AI takes on execution
2. How OpenAI thinks about building for model capabilities two to three months out
3. OpenAI’s best internal memes, such as “Is this maximally accelerated?” and “Are you mainlining it yet?”
4. Why ambition is the new bottleneck for companies, and why elevating others’ ambitions is now the key part of the PM job
5. Writing as thinking vs. writing as reporting
episodes.descriptionCN:
Tara Seshan 在 OpenAI 领导 Codex 和 ChatGPT Work 的产品（与之前的播客嘉宾 Andrew Ambrosino 一起，他是她的工程经理）。在 OpenAI 之前，Tara 在 Stripe 工作了六年多，她是该公司首批五名产品经理之一。她继续领导 Watershed 的产品，该产品被《时代》杂志评为 2022 年最佳发明之一，她也是创始人和 Thiel Fellow。对我个人来说最有意义的是：Tara 是首届 Lenny’s Newsletter Fellow 的三名成员之一，这是我几年前运行的一个项目，旨在关注最令人兴奋的新兴产品领导者。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 从“划船”到“掌舵”的转变，以及为什么随着人工智能的执行，人类的判断力和野心将成为差异化因素
2. OpenAI 如何考虑两到三个月后的模型能力构建
3. OpenAI 最好的内部模因，例如“这是最大加速吗？”和“你已经把它主线化了吗？”
4. 为什么野心是公司的新瓶颈，为什么提升他人的野心现在是 PM 工作的关键部分
5. 作为思考写作与作为报告写作

episodes.title: How to close $100K+ enterprise deals, step by step | Jen Abel
episodes.description:
Jen Abel is the co-founder of JJellyfish and GM of enterprise sales at State Affairs. She is widely regarded as one of the sharpest practitioners in enterprise sales, and for that reason, this is her third visit to the podcast. In our first conversation we went deep on founder-led sales; in our second we mapped the $1M–$10M playbook. This time we do something I’ve never seen on another podcast: walk step by step through the full enterprise sales cycle. Most people think it’s five steps. Jen shows it’s closer to 15.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why the standard five-stage CRM pipeline is a forecasting tool, not a sales process, and what the real 15-step cycle looks like
2. The “pincer model” for landing the first meeting at the executive and N-minus-one level simultaneously
3. How to craft a two-to-three-sentence message around giving them “alpha”
4. How to run an intro call that extracts maximum intelligence before you ever show a demo
5. The two-to-three-day pilot structure, how to define success jointly, and when to charge for a longer pilot versus giving it away
6. Navigating pricing, procurement, redline negotiations, and the final signature without losing momentum
episodes.descriptionCN:
Jen Abel 是 JJellyfish 的联合创始人兼国务部企业销售总经理。她被广泛认为是企业销售领域最敏锐的从业者之一，因此，这是她第三次访问该播客。在我们的第一次谈话中，我们深入探讨了创始人主导的销售；在第二个例子中，我们绘制了 100 万美元至 1000 万美元的剧本。这次我们做了一些我在其他播客中从未见过的事情：一步步走过整个企业销售周期。大多数人认为这是五个步骤。 Jen 表示已经接近 15 了。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么标准的五阶段 CRM 管道是预测工具，而不是销售流程，以及真正的 15 步循环是什么样的
2、首次会议同时落地高管层和N-1层的“夹击模式”
3. 如何围绕给他们“阿尔法”制定两到三句话的信息
4. 如何在演示之前运行一次介绍性通话以获取最大程度的情报
5. 两到三天的试点结构，如何共同定义成功，以及何时对较长的试点收费而不是免费
6. 在不失去动力的情况下完成定价、采购、红线谈判和最终签署

episodes.title: OpenAI’s Head of Design: This is the best time in history to be a designer | Ian Silber
episodes.description:
Ian Silber is the head of product design at OpenAI, where he has led the design of ChatGPT, Codex, and all of OpenAI’s product experience for the past three years. Before OpenAI, he was at Artifact, the AI-powered news app built by the founders of Instagram. Prior to that, he spent eight years at Instagram, where he worked on products including Reels. Ian is one of the most consequential designers working in AI today, and he takes us inside how OpenAI designs ChatGPT, Codex, and the future of how we will interact with AI.
In our in-depth conversation, we discuss:
1. Why Ian believes this is the best time in history to be a product designer
2. Why engineers 10x’d with AI but design teams haven’t
3. What OpenAI looks for when hiring designers
4. “Just do less”: Ian’s counterintuitive advice to his designers
5. The future of ChatGPT as a super app
6. Where humans still win: user understanding, invention, and point of view
episodes.descriptionCN:
Ian Silber 是 OpenAI 的产品设计主管，过去三年他领导了 ChatGPT、Codex 的设计以及 OpenAI 的所有产品体验。在加入 OpenAI 之前，他曾在 Artifact 工作，这是一款由 Instagram 创始人开发的人工智能新闻应用程序。在此之前，他在 Instagram 工作了八年，负责开发包括 Reels 在内的产品。 Ian 是当今人工智能领域最有影响力的设计师之一，他带我们了解 OpenAI 如何设计 ChatGPT、Codex，以及我们与人工智能交互的未来。
在我们的深入对话中，我们讨论：
1. 为什么 Ian 认为这是历史上成为产品设计师的最佳时代
2. 为什么工程师十倍地使用人工智能，但设计团队却没有
3. OpenAI 在招聘设计师时看重什么
4.“少做一点”：伊恩给设计师的违反直觉的建议
5. ChatGPT 作为超级应用程序的未来
6. 人类仍然获胜的地方：用户理解、发明和观点

episodes.title: 🔬Bio-security is an AI Arms Race - Eric Nguyen (CEO, Radical Numerics)
episodes.description:
What happens when AI stops merely *reading* DNA and starts learning how to *write* it? Eric Nguyen, CEO and co-founder of Radical Numerics and a key figure behind Evo, joins us to explain the leap from early genome language models to Omni—a system that can outperform specialized models on disease-variant prediction, reason across biological sequences, and even begin to “show its work” when designing better molecules. The surprising part is *where those capabilities seem to be coming from*: in several cases, the model learns useful biological structure it was never explicitly taught.
But the same capability creates a much harder question: what happens when models can design sequences that preserve biological function while looking different enough to evade today’s defenses? Eric walks us through why current biosecurity systems may be solving the wrong problem, what an AI-native defense could look like, and why the teams pushing biological design forward may also need to build the systems that defend against it. The YouTube version is especially worth watching—we put Radical Numerics’ benchmark results and model visualizations on screen as Eric walks through what they actually show.

episodes.title: 🔬 Google's AI Scientist Started as an Attempt to Automate Kaggle — John Platt, Google Fellow
episodes.description:
From inventing textbook machine learning algorithms to winning an Academy Award and discovering two asteroids, John Platt has spent his career at the intersection of computation and science. In this episode, the Google Fellow joins Latent Space to unpack how AI can accelerate scientific discovery, what it takes to turn a research problem into something an agent can optimize, and why better models still need scientists who know how to avoid fooling themselves.
We go deep on Google’s Empirical Research Assistance (ERA): an AI research system that grew out of an attempt to automate Kaggle, combines LLMs with tree search to improve experiments, and helped crack a climate modeling problem that had stalled for years. John explains the leap from Gemini 2.0 to 2.5, the dangers of reward hacking, and how AI can help reduce airplane contrail warming and detect wildfires. We also explore fusion, quantum computing, the early days of neural networks, studying under Richard Feynman, and why developing scientific taste still means doing some things the hard way.
We discuss:
- John’s Academy Award, two asteroid discoveries, and the legacy of Platt scaling and SMO
- ERA: how an “auto-Kaggle” idea became a system for scientific research
- Turning scientific problems into scoreable tasks—and why choosing the score is the hard part
- How LLMs, tree search, and Upper Confidence Bound guide experimental iteration
- The Gemini 2.0-to-2.5 inflection that made the approach work
- Why predictive accuracy doesn’t automatically mean scientific understanding
- Reward hacking, Goodhart’s law, and the half-pixel labeling error that helped win a Kaggle competition

- How airplane contrails trap heat, and why small changes in flight altitude can help

- Why domain expertise, hands-on experimentation, and scientific taste matter in the age of AI
- John’s 20% time rule for learning, and what gets lost when everything is optimized
- The future of human scientists—and Feynman’s enduring advice about not fooling yourself

episodes.description:
From their seed led by Nat Friedman and Dan Gross, AIUC has now announced a monster $40M Series A! From being Anthropic’s first product hire to building the standards, testing, and insurance infrastructure meant to make frontier AI deployable, Rune Kvist is betting that the biggest constraint on AI adoption won’t be capability — it will be trust. In this episode, the AIUC cofounder joins swyx and Vibhu to announce a new $40M round and explain why companies like Cursor, Harvey, Lovable, and ElevenLabs are increasingly confronting a problem that gets harder as AI gets better: who is responsible when autonomous systems fail?
We go deep on AIUC-1, the emerging standard for agent security, safety, and reliability; how AI agents are stress-tested for jailbreaks, hallucinations, and data leaks; and why Rune thinks standards and insurance could become critical infrastructure for AI. episodes.description:
From helping pioneer ideas that foreshadowed prompt-based, general-purpose NLP to now building AI systems that can automate AI research itself, Richard Socher is betting that the next major step in AI is recursive self-improvement. In this episode, Richard joins Latent Space to unpack his vision for the “Eureka Machine”: a superintelligence that can improve the process of invention itself, accelerate AI research, and eventually tackle major problems across science, energy, materials, biology, and more.
Pre-order the book "The Eureka Machine" here:
Richard is the founder of Recursive, You.com, & AIX Ventures. We go deep on Recursive’s early results, including an AI research system that Richard says outperformed humans and their agents on optimization tasks in less than two days, as well as work on NVIDIA GPU kernels where the system discovered improvements without relying on a team of CUDA experts.
We also explore the harder questions around increasingly capable AI: reward hacking, whether Anthropic-style constitutions actually work, AI regulation and proposals to “pace” frontier development, open-source models as geopolitical soft power, whether today’s LLM paradigm is enough, and what happens if AI systems eventually begin choosing their own goals. Richard reflects on the rejected research that helped inspire later GPT work, open-endedness, the AI Economist, simulations of entire economies, and his framework for thinking about the upper bounds of intelligence itself.
We discuss:
• The Eureka Machine and Richard’s vision for an AI that can automate invention
• Why Richard is optimistic about superintelligence for science and technology
• Why AI hard-takeoff scenarios may underestimate physical and economic constraints

episodes.description:
In 1984, the Walt Disney Company was worth more dead than alive. Disney Animation — the heart of Walt's famous flywheel — had stagnated for years, bleeding away talent while corporate raiders circled, salivating over offers to sell off the film library to MGM and offload the parks to hotel operators. But what followed instead was the greatest turnaround in media history under Michael Eisner and Frank Wells. Beauty and the Beast. The Lion King. Broadway. Bringing the Disney Vault home on VHS and DVD. And the greatest media acquisition of all time — ESPN.
And then... it all almost fell apart. Again. Euro Disney turned into a money pit. Boardroom and executive infighting ran rampant. Animation descended into a dumpster fire. (Remember Chicken Little? Us neither.) Comcast — Comcast!! — tried to steal the company via a hostile takeover. Out of the chaos, a new generation of Disney management emerged under Bob Iger to stage yet another epic comeback with Pixar, Marvel and Lucasfilm, creating the defining media empire of the 21st century…until the tech companies came along. Tune in for the ultimate Acquired thrill ride: Disney, Part II.

episodes.title: The Accidental Genius of the Disney Vault
episodes.description: In 1944, Disney accidentally created one of the greatest business strategies in entertainment history: they re-released Snow White in theaters seven years after its debut. Because home video didn't exist, an entirely new generation of kids experienced the film for the first time, birthing the "Disney Vault." Disney still relies on this 6-8-year cadence today (more in the form of sequels than re-releases today) to keep their core IP culturally dominant without over-saturating the market.
episodes.descriptionCN: 1944 年，迪士尼意外地创造了娱乐史上最伟大的商业策略之一：《白雪公主》在首映七年后重新在影院上映。由于家庭录像不存在，全新一代的孩子第一次体验了这部电影，诞生了“迪士尼金库”。如今，迪士尼仍然依靠这种 6-8 年的节奏（更多地以续集而不是重新发布的形式）来保持其核心 IP 在文化上的主导地位，同时避免市场过度饱和。

episodes.title: AI Software Factories
episodes.description:
“Clearly there are 100x or 1,000x engineers now. The world hasn’t adjusted.”
— Guillermo Rauch (Vercel)
Guillermo: I’ve been really pilled with this idea of software factories. You used to ship the output directly, and everything inside the company was how good is person A at shipping output B? And now what’s happening is the way that I’m judging you as an engineer is, are you producing the factory that will produce multiplicative outputs B through Z, right?
We used to believe, and it used to be somewhat controversial, that there’s 10X engineers. Now clearly there’s 100X or 1,000X engineers. And the world hasn’t fully adjusted to this.
@naval: I used to get flamed on Twitter for saying there are 10X engineers, because it flies in the face of so much equality philosophy that everyone’s equal. But the reality is, when you’re operating in idea domains—when you’re operating in intellectual domains and virtual digital domains—it’s not even 10X. It’s 100X or 1,000X, and it always has been.
Satoshi, Notch, the guy who invented JavaScript, the Brendan Eichs of the world. John Carmack. These are 1,000X programmers.
Not to even mention if you choose the right thing to work on versus the wrong thing to work on, that’s an infinity difference. And it could just be not necessarily even a better programmer, just one who had a better judgment of what to work on in the first place.
And now obviously it’s less controversial, because of AI leverage.
episodes.descriptionCN:
“显然现在有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有调整。”
— 吉列尔莫·劳赫 (Vercel)
Guillermo：我对软件工厂的想法非常着迷。你以前直接运送输出，公司内部的一切都是A在运送输出B时有多好？现在发生的事情是我对你作为一名工程师的评价，你是否正在生产将产生乘法输出 B 到 Z 的工厂，对吧？
我们曾经相信，有 10X 工程师的存在，但也曾经存在一些争议。现在显然有 100 倍或 1,000 倍的工程师。世界还没有完全适应这一点。
@naval：我曾经因为说有 10X 工程师而在 Twitter 上受到攻击，因为它违背了人人平等的平等理念。但现实是，当你在创意领域运作时——当你在知识领域和虚拟数字领域运作时——它甚至不是 10 倍。它是 100 倍或 1,000 倍，而且一直都是。
Satoshi，Notch，JavaScript 的发明者，世界上的 Brendan Eichs。约翰·卡马克.这些是 1000 倍的程序员。
更不用说你选择正确的工作还是错误的工作，这是一个无穷大的差异。而且不一定是更好的程序员，只是一个对首先要做什么有更好判断的人。
现在，由于人工智能的影响力，它的争议显然减少了。

In this solo episode, I explain why I expect a wave of one-person businesses built as AI-native service firms, and I show you how I built one. Three things matured at the same time: specialist creative models, Astra as an orchestrator that plans and repairs work, and the Higgsfield API, which puts 50+ creative models behind one key. I demo Studio Operator, the MVP I built to show you how I’d run an AI-native creative Agency, and I walk through the six prompts I used to build it. I finish with a model-by-model primer, three startup ideas, and four filters for choosing which firm to build.

- Creative models, Astra, and one production API matured together, and that makes one-person creative firms possible now.
- Upwork, Fiverr, and Contra show what buyers purchase again and again, so I start from validated demand.
- I estimate AI-native firms can reach 60%+ net margins, compared with 10–15% for a typical human agency.
- I built Studio Operator with six prompts, one layer of the firm per prompt, in a deliberate order.
- I match each job to a model: people, products, text, repairs, long scenes, speech, motion, or finishing.
- The strongest ideas pair a creative surface with a repetitive, checkable operational core.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Three Shifts at Once
Creative models like Kling, Flux, and Seedream moved far past the AI Will Smith spaghetti video. Astra can read a messy brief, plan the work, pick specialist models, track budget, and repair failures. The Higgsfield API puts the models, pricing, requests, and outputs behind one API, which replaces a dozen separate accounts.
2. Human Agency vs. AI-Native Firm
A traditional creative agency grows through word of mouth and organic social, and it nets 10–15% because hiring, turnover, and marketing eat the margin. An AI-native firm adds marketplaces like Upwork and Fiverr as a third sales channel and takes on $100 to $25,000 jobs at gross margins that can reach 70–95%. I call it semi-autonomous: AI does the work, and a person approves it.
3. The Learning Loop
In a human agency, lessons walk out the door with the people who learned them. In an AI-native firm, every job feeds a loop that raises quality and margin, and I expect higher exit multiples because the business runs more like software.
4. Inside Studio Operator
My dashboard shows 25 active jobs, a $3,400 pipeline, and $3,200 in estimated gross profit. For a blood orange aperitif image, the client pays $10, Higgsfield production costs about one cent, and my expected profit is $9.99; the five-second video costs about $0.70 and includes a marketplace channel fee, which I put at 5–15%. Autonomy settings cap spend per job, repair cost, and attempts per step, and client memory stores logos, colors, fonts, and rejected styles for accounts like Moro Coffee.
5. A Model Primer by Job
Before I pick a model, I ask four questions: image, video, or speech; new asset or repair; cheap exploration or final version; and what must stay fixed. Then I route: Soul for people, Seedream or Flux for products, Ideogram or Recraft for text and layout, Qwen for repairs, Seedance for longer scenes, Kling for hero shots, Wan or Minimax for speech, Kling Motion Control for copied movement, and Topaz plus finishing tools for delivery.
6. Three Startup Ideas
An always-on ad studio sells a weekly creative pack for one SKU, with prospects from the Meta Ad Library and a $750–$1,500 paid sprint that grows into a monthly package. A franchise localization service turns one approved national campaign into local versions for brands with 20–200 locations, starting with a paid five-location pilot. An industrial catalog service turns spec sheets and CAD files into demos, training clips, and sales graphics, starting in one vertical with prospects from ThomasNet and trade show exhibitor lists.

In this episode I speak with Nicolas Cole about the real value of everything you write on the internet. Cole has 15 years of experience as a nonfiction writer and ghostwriter, and he runs the SaaS platform Typeshare. He gives me a simple model with three tiers of content: commodity, personality, and original. He also explains the digital brain, which he calls your personal language model, and he shows how AI repeats your approved language at scale. By the end, you know how to judge the short, medium, and long-term value of a piece before you write it.

Key Points
• A point of view creates the moat, because copycats must wait for your next idea.
• Content sits in three tiers: commodity, personality, and original. Each tier adds different leverage.
• Ownership equals association. Volume builds it, and personality details make it strong.
• Your life story is the unmade data set, so AI learns it only from your own writing.
• Every piece sits on a spectrum from timely to timeless, so match your expectations to the type.
• Humans do the thinking and the writing. Robots do the repeating and the remixing.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Point Of View Moat
Cole answers the popular claim that AI removes the moat from SaaS. He says a moat appears when a product carries a method, such as Typeshare and its personal language model idea. A competitor who copies features must still look back at the person who does the thinking.
2. Language Is Open Source
Cole describes the alphabet, words, and most groupings of words as shared property. He uses the example of a health sentence that millions of people repeat. This explains why readers label some writing as AI slop: they recognize a commodity sentence.
3. The Three Tiers Of Content
Cole separates commodity content, personality content, and original content. Commodity content helps beginners, and it stays useful as a first step. Personality content and original content raise the long-term value of your library.
4. Approved Language And The Digital Brain

Cole puts every piece on a spectrum. A meme captures 24 hours of attention, and an essay serves you for ten years. He asks one question before you start: how much value do you extract, and over what time horizon?

Cole unbundles voice into word choice, sentence length, and sentence structure, so you can create it on purpose. He recalls a client edit of about one percent that made a piece sound like the client. Ryan shows how Jev takes an input plus an output schema and returns a probability for each choice in about 200 milliseconds. He demos Jev sorting 1,700 emails for 18 cents total, then covers lead scoring, support routing, video clipping, and browser control. • Ryan's demo scores 1,700 emails for 18 cents total.

• Keep Jev in an advisory role, and save frontier models for high-intelligence tasks like trading.

Numbered Section Summaries
1. What Jev Actually Is
Ryan explains Jev as a classifier. You define an input and an output schema, and Jev returns a probability for each option, for example 80% orange, 10% red, and 10% blue for the color of an iPhone.
2. The 18-Cent Email Demo
Ryan runs Jev on 1,700 of his own emails and scores each one for category, priority, spam score, and reply likelihood. The run uses 4.2 million input tokens and 500,000 output tokens and costs 18 cents total.
3. A Decision Model, Distinct From a Chat Model
Jev returns only structured output, meaning the numbers and categories from your schema, with zero visible reasoning. Developers can drop that type-safe output straight into code. Ryan also tests Jev as a letter-by-letter text generator to show how a decision model differs from a chat model.
4. Cheap Enough to Experiment
A $5 intro credit lasts Ryan's team two days of heavy use, and he estimates $10 could last about three months. His girlfriend's graphic design agency uses Jev to score contact-form leads on a scale from 0 to 1, so high-value leads get a fast reply.
5. The AI Traffic Cop
I frame Jev as a traffic cop: information comes in, and Jev decides what it is, how important it is, and what happens next. A high-confidence lead goes to a human, a lower score goes to automation or an LLM, and the lowest scores get ignored. Ryan adds support routing, where 200-millisecond answers replace slow streaming responses.

I ask how to find a business with an expensive queue of incoming information and put Jev at the front of it. Ryan describes a local services platform that matches a request like "I need my driveway power washed" to the best nearby business and turns "instant quote" forms into truly instant quotes.

Ryan's Bitcoin test, which asks Jev to buy, hold, or sell every minute, performs poorly. OpenAI's latest frontier model does a little better because it cross-references news. Ryan's advice: use Jev for routing-style decisions and keep it away from your portfolio.

Ryan's video clipper scores 17 moments in about three seconds, and he builds it in about 10 minutes. A Browser Use demo shows Jev picking a flight from Zurich to London in 7.1 seconds. I sit down with Remy to go through Instinct, the new invite-only personal agent that runs inside iMessage. Remy shares his raw chat history on screen: a haircut booking in Copenhagen, a restaurant reservation, a Bali visa on arrival, and an Emirates Skywards sign-up. We cover the parts that impress us, the points where the agent hits a wall, and the privacy questions that stay open. By the end of this episode you understand what Instinct does today, and you get fresh ideas for personal agents in general.

Key Points
• Instinct hides the agent complexity behind a phone number and iMessage, so a first-time user starts in seconds.
• Remy gets it to book a haircut, hold a restaurant table, file a Bali visa on arrival, and open an Emirates Skywards account.
• A spend-limited virtual card keeps the blast radius small when the agent pays for things.
• The agent stalls when a task needs a phone app or an Indonesian checkout page.
• Users report that Instinct keeps copies of email after they disconnect Google, so treat privacy as an open risk.
• The trusted person network lets one Instinct talk to another, which builds network effects into the agentic era.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. The Invite-Only Launch
Remy first sees Instinct on X, where large AI accounts talk about it. The site shows a wait list, so he grabs an invite code from a public tweet. Scarcity drives the curiosity, and Remy reads the rollout as a marketing play as much as a compute limit.
2. Onboarding Built for the Mass Market
Remy signs in with a phone number and lands straight in iMessage. The agent opens with photo examples: flight bookings, check-ins, smoothie orders, subscription cancellations. Remy teaches founders AI for a living, so he values a flow that skips MCPs, CLIs, and markdown files.
3. The Workspace, the Connectors, and the Vault
A simple web workspace sits beside the chat. It holds contact methods, connectors for email, Slack and Granola, and a vault for logins, cards, and addresses. Remy connects his email accounts and stays impressed by how much context Instinct pulls about him.
4. Real Tasks: Haircut, Restaurant, Visa
Remy asks for salons in Copenhagen. Instinct researches spots, pulls reviews, sends photos, emails the salon, and confirms the booking hours later. It then holds a table at Bistro Central, files the Bali visa on arrival and the arrival card, and opens an Emirates Skywards account with a saved password.
5. Human Touches: Reactions, Memory, and Game Pigeon
Instinct reacts to messages, reads a thumbs-up as approval, and uses loud effects and confetti. It recalls the monitor from an earlier chat and adds it to the visa arrival card. It even plays a round of Game Pigeon Cup Pong, which surprises us both.
6. Network Effects, Privacy, and the Ten-Billion Question
The founder Noah announces a trusted person network, so one Instinct can talk to another. I compare the invite rollout to Clubhouse in 2020, which raised at $4vbillion. I welcome Ras Mic back to the pod to explain the phrase "software factory." Mic shares his screen and walks through the exact system that he runs today. His factory has four steps: isolate, build, prove, and ship. He keeps the whole system in five or six markdown files, so it works with any model and any harness. By the end of this episode, you can boot up your own factory, run many agents in parallel, and trust the code that comes back.
Create your own Software Factory:
Timestamps
00:00 – Intro
02:17 – Software Factory Definition
03:44 – Why the Software Factory Matters
05:23 – Step 1: Isolate With Git Work Trees
11:34 – Step 2: Build With the Code Structure Skill
14:48 – Step 3: Prove With Evidence-Driven Testing
22:25 – Step 4: Ship With Grep Loop and Greptile
26:52 – The Physical Factory Analogy
29:21 – A Software Factory Is Markdown Files
30:02 – Closing Thoughts
Key Points
• A software factory is a workflow of skills and domain knowledge, so it runs with any model and any harness.
• Isolate: every feature starts in a fresh git work tree branched from origin main, so each agent keeps its own station.
• Build: a code structure skill makes the agent write service layer code that a human developer can read.
• Prove: the agent records a before state and an after state as video, screenshots, or numbers.
• Ship: Greptile scores the PR, and the agent loops back to build until it earns five out of five.
• Mic runs up to 15 features in parallel and reviews the visual proof instead of the raw code.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. What a Software Factory Means
Ras defines the term as a workflow, a set of skills, and domain knowledge, packed into markdown files. The word "factory" points to structure, speed, and a conveyor belt that keeps quality high. He is clear that a software factory is a method rather than a product you buy.
2. Why the Factory Matters Now
Model intelligence keeps rising, and Ras names GPT-6 Astra as his workhorse and the model with the lowest hallucination rate. A factory lets you use that intelligence in a systematic way, instead of typing back and forth with a chat window. He offers his own skills for free, and he asks people to understand the process first and then adapt it.
3. The Agents.md File as the Master Instruction
The agents.md file is a single markdown document that goes into the agent chat ahead of every message. Ras says most people fill it with facts the agent already reads from the code base. He fills his with a workflow instead, because the workflow is the part the agent lacks.
4. Step 1: Isolate
A skill called "new feature" starts each task in a fresh git work tree branched from origin main. A work tree acts like a copy of the app, and the agent merges it back later. This keeps two agents apart, so one agent leaves the other agent's files alone. Michael shows four terminal tabs running four features on the same app.
5. Step 2: Build
The code structure skill tells the agent to write in a service layer architecture. Models get the job done, and they often get it done in a sloppy way, so the skill supplies the guideline. The result stays readable for a hired developer, for Michael, and for any fresh agent that opens the code base later.
6. Step 3: Prove
Two skills handle proof: evidence-driven testing and before and after. The agent records the broken state, does the work, and records the working state, then embeds both in the PR. When the after shot shows a gap, the agent sends itself back to the build step on its own. For work with an invisible surface, such as performance, the agent supplies numbers: one page went from 815 milliseconds to about 61.
7. Step 4: Ship
The grep loop skill sends the PR to Greptile, a third-party code review agent, and Greptile returns feedback plus a confidence score. A three out of five sends the agent back through build, prove, and ship. Ras steps in at five out of five and clicks merge. He mentions Code Rabbit and Macroscope as alternatives.
8. The Factory Analogy and the Case for Code Review
I map the four steps onto a real factory: a custom order gets its own station, the assembly line builds it, quality control tests it, and shipping sends it out the door. Ras agrees, and he says he may rename his skills to match.

• Ras went from a speaker idea to a $561 parts order and a merged pull request in about 30 minutes.

• The shift that vibe coding brought to software now reaches physical products.
Numbered Section Summaries
1. Why This Review Skips the Demos Ras opens with the reason for this format. The viral Astra clips show games and 3D scenes, and those stay fun to watch. We spend the episode on work that pays: better code, better products, and new businesses.
2. Price, Speed, and Two Audits Astra sits at OpenAI's top price and matches Fable. A Codex subscription covers most of that cost today, and the model finishes tasks in fewer steps. Ras recommends two prompts for any live app: a full performance review, and a security audit.
3. Reference Images and Computer Use Ras gets his best UI results when he gives Astra a reference image, and he used the old Microsoft XP network icon for one design. He also rates the computer-use ability highly. He pointed Codex at the Canada Revenue Agency site, and it found pages that Google search missed.

The first three serve solo operators: a bill renegotiator that talks to provider chat support, a service-business teardown that turns an agency workflow into a $500–$5,000 per month software product, and a marketplace watcher that texts me every underpriced listing in my city.
5. Agents for Operations and Growth The next six prompts run a company. A weekly operator dashboard reads my docs, Stripe exports, and calls, then names the three highest-leverage actions. An agent-opportunity audit ranks tasks by human hours saved within 30 days. A browser operator returns an SOP, a nightly QA agent opens my app on a real phone, a competitor agent reports monthly, and a browser game captures leads for the core product.
